item.title: Llama-modchip: 284B DeepSeek on 64GB RAM, no GPU
item.abstract:
llama-modchip (v2.4.0) CPU-First Inference for 284B & 30B Mixture-of-Experts Models on 16–64 GB RAM Quickstart · Quantization & Memory Specs · Supported Models · Supported Hardware · Leaderboard · Technical Paper ( paper/ ) · Architecture · FAQ 284.33B Total MoE params (13.17B active) 56.56 GiB DeepSeek-V4 GGUF (1.71 bpw) 57.61 GiB Peak VmRSS @ 256K ctx 44.36 tok/s 284B CPU prefill (16C Zen 5) 25.0–111.6 tok/s 30B MoE CPU decode (3.75 bpw) 13.1 ms /dev/shm KV slot restore 0 GPUs required Hardware Class System RAM Target Checkpoint Throughput (0 GPUs) Architecture & Memory Notes Developer laptop / Mini-PC 16–32 GB Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B ( 14.35 GiB , 3.75 bpw ) 25.0–60.4 tok/s 46 Mamba-2 SSM layers + 1.64 MB L3 PVS drafter; 256K context uses 432 MB KV 64 GB Desktop / Server 64 GB DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B ( 56.56 GiB , 1.71 bpw ) 44.4 tok/s pp · 9.1–14.7 tok/s tg Fits in 62.5 GiB usable Linux RAM (57.61 GiB VmRSS) with zero NVMe swap Hybrid Desktop (CPU + 16 GB GPU) 32–64 GB Nemotron-30B / Qwen3-30B ( 3.75–4.25 bpw ) 80.80 tok/s Hot attention/SSM trunk on GPU ( -ngl 99 ), cold routed MoE experts in CPU RAM 8-Channel Workstation (Threadripper) 128 GB+ DeepSeek-284B / Nemotron-30B 111.62 tok/s (30B) 8-CCD AVX-512BW _1x8 register tiling saturates 8-channel DDR5 bandwidth Overview llama-modchip is a set of ggml / llama.cpp kernel patches, quantization transcoders, and runtime tools designed to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) checkpoints entirely in system RAM on x86_64 ( AVX-512 / AVX2 ) and ARM64 ( NEON / SVE / Apple Metal) processors: Fitting 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash into 64 GB Physical RAM ( 56.56 GiB on disk, 1.71 bpw ): Standard UD-IQ1_S builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash ( 284.33B total, 13.17B active across 43 MLA layers and 256 routed experts) occupy 76.87 GiB ( 82.5 GB ), exceeding the ~62.5 GiB of usable RAM on a 64 GB Linux system and causing page-cache thrashing or OOM kills. llama-modchip reduces the checkpoint to 56.56 GiB ( 60.73 GB ) so the entire model plus a 256K KV cache ( 57.61–58.9 GiB VmRSS ) locks into RAM with zero swap. By default, all 6 routed experts per layer ( Top-6 ) are evaluated without pruning. CPU Cache & SIMD Kernel Patches ( +77% prefill, +53% decode): Replaces single-column quantized matrix-vector loops during prompt prefill with a 4-level register ( ZMM AVX-512BW) + L1D ( 32 KB ) + L2 ( 1 MB ) + L3 ( 64 MB ) multi-column ( {8,4,3,2} ) tiling schedule ( 25.0 -> 44.36 tok/s on 16-core Zen 5), register-stationary MQA8 FlashAttention, and non-temporal _MM_HINT_NTA MoE streaming so cold expert weights do not evict hot KV cache lines from L3. Self-Speculative Drafting & Instant Agent Context Restore: Pairs a 1.64 MB L2/L3 Zobrist n-gram drafter ( Stockfish-PVS v2 ) with /dev/shm KV slot snapshots ( 13.1–32.6 ms restore time for 40-tool Claude Code prompts) and an $O(1)$ speculative rollback fix for deepseek4 recurrent/MLA states. Quantization & Memory Breakdown To answer the most common technical question upfront— exact bit-widths ( bpw ), base checkpoints, and what is compressed in each GGUF : Checkpoint Total / Active Params Base Source Disk Size ( GiB / GB ) Effective bpw Layer-by-Layer Tensor Allocation Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Q4_0 30.2B / 3.0B BF16 Official 17.59 GiB ( 18.89 GB ) 4.50 bpw Standard Q4_0 across MoE + attention; F32 norms & SSM conv/decay Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-MXFP4 30.2B / 3.0B BF16 Official 15.95 GiB ( 17.13 GB ) 4.25 bpw GGML_TYPE_MXFP4 ( E2M1 + shared exponent) on routed MoE; Q4_0 / Q8_0 trunk Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64 30.2B / 3.0B BF16 Official 14.35 GiB ( 15.41 GB ) 3.75 bpw Attention, Mamba-2 SSM & shared experts in Q4_0 / Q8_0 / F32 ; cold routed MoE experts in hybrid Q4_0 + Fractal-64 ( Q2_0 , 64-weight block + BF16 scale). Scores 100/100 on benchmarks/eval_quality_and_tools.py . DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal 284.33B / 13.17B Unsloth UD-IQ1_S ( 76.87 GiB / 82.5 GB ) 56.56 GiB ( 60.73 GB ) 1.71 bpw • Embeddings, Dense L0, 43 Shared Experts ( shexp ), MLA kv_a / q_a / wkv_b : Preserved in Q4_K / Q5_K / F32 • MLA wq_b & attn_output ( wo_a / wo_b ): Transcoded to Fractal-64 ( GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 , 3.75 bpw , 30B/64-block w/ 8 sub-scales & BF16 scale) • 256 Routed MoE Experts ( ffn_*_exps ): Primarily IQ1_S ( 1.5625 bpw ) with analytical SwiGLU-H2 second-order scale matching; sensitive boundary layers preserved in IQ2_XXS ( 2.06 bpw ) & IQ1_M ( 1.75 bpw ) ( -20.31 GiB vs UD-IQ1_S ) Note on MoE Expert Routing ( Top-K ): By default ( v2.4.0 Lossless ), DeepSeek-V4-Flash evaluates all 6 routed experts + 1 shared expert ( Top-6 ) per layer with zero expert dropping ( 1.00000 logit cosine similarity vs the unpatched runtime on the same checkpoint). Setting LLAMA_MOE_TOP_K=5 or 4 is an optional runtime flag for users who want to trade a small perplexity delta for higher decode throughput. Quickstart Linux & macOS (Automated Setup & Chat) git clone https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip.git cd llama-modchip
./modchip chat Direct Run (Pre-Compiled Linux x86_64 Binary + Hugging Face .gguf ) Compatibility Note ( GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 = 40 ): Fractal-64 models use custom block-64 BF16 -scale tensors ( GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 , type ID 40 ) and deepseek4 / Stockfish-PVS kernels. Unpatched llama.cpp , Ollama, or LM Studio binaries will reject them with unknown tensor type 40 . Use ./modchip above or the standalone pre-compiled binary ( llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 , zero external .so dependencies) included in the Hugging Face repositories and GitHub Release v2.4.0 : # 1. For 30B Nemotron-3.5-A3B (14.35 GiB — runs in 16–32 GB RAM at 25–60.4 tok/s): hf download Synchopate/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64-CPU-GGUF \ llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64.gguf --local-dir . chmod +x llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64
./llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 -m NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64.gguf -c 262144 -t 16 --port 8080 # 2. For 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash (56.56 GiB — fits in 64 GB RAM at 9.1–14.7 tok/s): hf download Synchopate/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal-64GB-CPU-GGUF --local-dir ./dsv4
chmod +x ./dsv4/llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64
./dsv4/llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 -m ./dsv4/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal-00001-of-00003.gguf -c 32768 -t 16 -fa on --port 8080 Windows 10/11 (Hybrid GPU + CPU MoE Pack) Open windows/ and run windows/AVVIA_MODCHIP.bat (or ./modchip start in Git Bash). It detects physical CPU cores, free RAM, and GPU VRAM ( nvidia-smi ), downloads llama.cpp CUDA 12.4 / Vulkan binaries, computes the --n-cpu-moe split, and launches the Web Chat UI ( http://127.0.0.1:8080 ). ./modchip Command Description ./modchip chat Interactive terminal chat with live tok/s , TTFT, and Stockfish-PVS acceptance telemetry ./modchip web Opens the Dark-Mode Web Chat & Live Telemetry HUD ( http://127.0.0.1:8787 ) ./modchip bench Runs a 30-second 2-stage speed test and prints a shareable CPU Benchmark Scorecard ./modchip claude Launches Claude Code CLI ( 40 tools ) wired to the local 256K engine ( 18.9–32.6 ms warm restore) ./modchip eval Runs the reproducible 100-Point Quality, Tool-Calling, Coding & 8.5K Needle Gate ./modchip quantize Transcodes BF16 / Q4_0 / UD-IQ1_S GGUFs into Fractal-64 ( 3.75 bpw ) or Fractal-MXFP4 ( 4.25 bpw ) ./modchip status / stop Inspects CPU readiness, 2MB HugePages , and /dev/shm IPC, or stops background services Hardware Readiness Check (Zero Model Download Required) curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/main/scripts/check_cpu_readiness.py | python3 Submit your terminal scorecard via a GitHub Benchmark Issue or GitHub Discussions to add your CPU to the leaderboard below. Supported Models & Model-Specific Optimizations Each model family has a dedicated technical guide with mathematical derivations, operator-level latency profiles, and quality gate benchmarks: Model Family Total / Active Params Disk ( GGUF ) & 256K RAM ( VmRSS ) Key Optimizations Implemented Verified Speed ( 16C Zen 5 / Hybrid) Detailed Guide NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.

item.title: How to Run NVIDIA Dory 4B with llama.cpp: Loop by Loop Guide
item.abstract: In this tutorial, we work with Dory 1.0 4B , a small reasoning model from NVIDIA’s Nemotron Labs whose middle layers form a shared block that can be applied once, twice, three, or four times for every token. Each extra pass, or loop, spends more computation per token without adding a single parameter, so one checkpoint can run at four different compute budgets with no retraining. We build the llama.cpp branch that NVIDIA’s model card pins, download the 3.7 GB GGUF, and read the architecture straight from the file to predict what each loop should cost in parameters and cache memory. We then check those predictions against the running server, measure decode speed at every loop count, test whether the cheaper last-loop cache changes the model’s predictions, and run a paired GSM8K evaluation to see how accuracy, answer length, and time per solved question move as the loops increase. We build llama-server from the exact commit of the Dory branch that NVIDIA’s model card pins, because Dory support in llama.cpp is still an open draft pull request and no released binary can load the model. The cell detects the platform and passes the card’s Metal flags on a Mac, or compiles CUDA kernels for the attached GPU alone on Colab, skipping the flash-attention kernels that the card’s –flash-attn off never uses, which keeps a T4 build manageable. It then checks that the checked-out commit is the pinned one, so every later number traces to one known version of the code. The Q5_K_M GGUF comes from Hugging Face at a fixed repository revision, and we hash it before anything else touches it. The card’s commands refer to the file as dory-q5_k_m.gguf, but the repository names it NVIDIA-Nemotron-Labs-Dory1.0-4B-Q5_K_M.gguf, so copying the card’s command verbatim fails; pinning the real name, the size, and the SHA-256 together catches both a wrong file and a corrupted download. The 3.67 GB file matches the card’s published checksum exactly, so every measurement that follows uses the same bytes NVIDIA published. The GGUF header tells us how the model is wired before we load it. Dory’s 72 layer entries split into an input group of 16, a shared recurrent group of 40 and an output group of 16, alternating attention and MLP, with one full-attention layer for every three sliding-window layers. Summing tensor sizes by group shows the recurrent block accounts for 1.84 of the model’s 3.98 billion parameters. The header also carries a trap: its built-in loop count is 4, while the card recommends 2, so a server started without an override silently runs the most expensive setting. From those group sizes, we can predict what a loop costs before running anything. A token passes through the input block, the recurrent block once per loop, the output block, and the LM head, so 4 loops apply 2.51 times the parameters of 1 loop and read 2.28 times the weight bytes, the better guide for a memory-bound decoder. The KV cache follows the fork’s allocation rule: per_loop keeps a separate cache for every loop of every recurrent attention layer, growing from 306 MiB at 1 loop to 816 MiB at 4 for a 4,096-token context, while last_loop stays at 306 MiB. Loop count and cache mode are read when the model loads, so each setting needs its own server process; the DoryServer helper starts one per configuration, waits for the health check, and parses the KV-cache lines from the server’s log. We compare the parsed layer counts with the prediction to prove an override actually took effect, rather than trusting the flag. We also start one server without any override as a negative control, and send one chat request to see how the server separates the model’s reasoning from its answer. With the helper in place, we start a server for each of seven settings, one to four loops in both cache modes, and record the measured KV memory next to the prediction. Decode speed comes from the server’s own timings on a fixed prompt, generating 192 tokens greedily three times and keeping the median, so the only thing that changes between rows is the loop setting. Dividing the one-loop speed by each row’s speed gives the measured slowdown, which we set beside the predicted ratios to see whether decoding behaves as compute-bound or memory-bound. Comparisons between settings are only meaningful if the measurements repeat and the accelerated build computes the same model as the reference CPU path. Two chat requests with the same seed at the card’s sampling temperature must return identical messages, otherwise per-question comparisons would mix model behaviour with sampling noise. We then start a CPU-only server, with no layers offloaded, and compare the most likely next token on five prompts against the GPU or Metal server, because Dory support has not been reviewed upstream on every backend. Next-token distributions show what a loop changes inside the model at almost no cost. For 50 GSM8K questions used as raw prompts, we request the top 20 next-token candidates under each setting and compare them by top-1 agreement and total-variation distance. The fork’s code implies a sharp prediction: last_loop overwrites a recurrent layer’s cache on every loop, so it can differ from per_loop only when earlier chunks of the prompt keep just their final-loop keys, which never happens when the whole prompt fits in one micro-batch. Repeating the probe with 16-token micro-batches tests exactly that. The paired GSM8K evaluation asks the same seeded sample of questions under five settings, with reasoning on, the card’s sampling settings and a fixed seed per question, so each question meets the same conditions at every loop count. For every reply, we record correctness against the dataset’s final answer, the number of generated tokens (including reasoning), whether the reply hit the 2,048-token limit, and the wall time. Results go to one JSONL file per setting as they arrive, so an interrupted Colab session resumes where it stopped. Thirty paired questions cannot settle small accuracy differences, so the statistics cell is built to say what the sample can and cannot show. Accuracy comes with Wilson intervals, and each contrast uses an exact McNemar test on the questions that only one setting solved. Token counts are compared as the median of per-question ratios against one loop, with a bootstrap interval, which tests the card’s claim that more loops need fewer generated tokens. Time per solved question combines speed, length, and accuracy into the number a user actually pays for. Rather than restate the model card, we check its claims against this run. Each row pairs a sentence from the card with the measurement that tests it: cache-size claims and the loop defaults to token efficiency and the accuracy of last-loop caching, and the verdict comes from the saved results rather than being typed by hand. Claims the notebook cannot reach, such as the benchmark table, the 256K context and the NVFP4 pre-training, are listed as untested rather than quietly dropped. The summary prints each step’s one-line result and every check the run decided, marking which passed and which failed, along with the fork commit, the GGUF revision, and the backend, so the notebook doubles as a record of exactly what was verified and on which hardware. In conclusion, Dory turns test-time compute into a load-time setting: one 3.7 GB file runs as four different models, from a single pass through its 20-block recurrent core to four, and the GGUF header alone predicts what each setting costs in parameters and cache memory. The notebook checks those predictions against the server, measures speed, tests the last-loop cache against a precise prediction from the code, and evaluates accuracy and answer length on a paired GSM8K sample. Two practical lessons hold whatever the measurements show: always set the loop count explicitly, because the GGUF defaults to four, and pin the fork commit, because Dory support in llama.cpp is still an open draft. Check out the FULL CODES here .

item.title: Google AI Releases Elephant-Goldfish Model Plugin for Spec-First Coding
item.abstract: Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin , a design-and-review layer for AI coding agents. The Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin makes an agent write a specification before it writes code. Fresh subagents with no conversation history then attack that spec. Google says thousands of its engineers use it . It is quite simple: catch wrong assumptions in a Markdown file, not in a pull request. EGM is an Apache 2.0 plugin of skills, reviewer personas and document standards. It is not a new language model. The method comes from Dave Rensin’s essay on elephants and goldfish. The Google Open Source blog frames it as a fix for AI “slop” and session context collapse. The README states it is not an officially supported Google product . The Elephant is a long session holding project context and earlier decisions. It drafts the spec and writes no code. Each Goldfish is a stateless subagent. It reads only the draft and the files it references. You resolve trade-offs and approve the design. /egm-drift-report later compares code with the spec. The docs recommend running it weekly. The review skill runs 5 sequential stages: Each stage allows at most 1 re-audit. Findings are ranked Blocker, Major or Nit. If a host has no subagent tool, EGM stops. A same-context review is not a Goldfish review. Launch coverage described Antigravity-only support , with more coming. The current harness guide covers Antigravity CLI and App, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT, omp and Muse. Antigravity CLI, Claude Code and Codex pass automated end-to-end fixtures. Claude Code needs version 2.1.271 or later . Reviewers there get only Read, Grep and Glob tools. CLAUDE.md files are excluded from their context. The test record gives concrete run data: EGM’s distinct move is reviewing the spec with zero-context agents. Spec Kit and Kiro center on human review between phases. Superpowers isolates subagents mainly at implementation time. Check out the GitHub repo , the project site and the Google Open Source blog post . item.title: Nous Research Releases Arete-27B that Cuts Qwen3.8-27B Propaganda From 22% to 0.9%
item.abstract: Nous Research has released Arete-27B , a supervised fine-tune of Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-27B . Arete-27B is a 27B open-weight model that strips Chinese state framing from Qwen’s answers. On Nous’s own 803-prompt eval, answers containing propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Developers get Qwen-class agentic skill without state-aligned answers. The weights, eval and training data are all public. Arete-27B is Qwen3.8-27B after supervised fine-tuning only . Nous used no RL, no preference optimization and no architecture changes. The license is Apache 2.0, matching the base model. Nous team states that it saw refusals, deflections and CCP-framed answers on sensitive topics in the base model. It picked Qwen3.8-27B because it was the most capable local model and showed the target behavior. The teacher was Inkling , an open model from Thinking Machines. Nous chose an open teacher to avoid terms-of-use limits on distillation. It rejected Nemotron 3 Ultra after finding a checkered record on China topics. Training covered about 52.8 million tokens at 64k context, without sequence packing. The run took 2 epochs and 1,202 steps at batch size 48. It used AdamW, a 1e-5 peak learning rate and tensor parallel 4. All language-model weights were trained. The vision encoder stayed frozen, since the data is text-only. The multi-token-prediction head was disabled. The released arete-data-pairs set holds 34,878 prompts across 7 topics. Each prompt has both an Inkling answer and a Qwen answer. 29,236 accepted teacher answers form the SFT split. The Propaganda_Eval set has 803 prompts across 7 value categories. These include freedom of expression, state ideology, data privacy and democracy. Each prompt carries 2 to 4 required facts from a cited source. A Grok 4.7 judge grades two things separately: The judge must quote the exact phrase to flag propaganda. Nous removed every training prompt that overlapped the eval. The eval is MIT licensed and includes grading scripts. On the model card page , Arete-27B raised fact mean from 2.32 to 2.98. Propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Answers scoring 0 dropped from 359 to 216 of 803. The biggest change came in freedom of expression. Fact score rose from 0.89 to 2.44, and propaganda fell from 60% to 1%. Capability held on Nous’s tests. Hermes Bench moved from 65.77% to 65.60%, which Nous calls noise. Terminal-Bench-2.1 rose from 67% to 70% in Nous’s harness. Nous does not claim credit for that gain. Note: Arete and Qwen ran at temperature 0 in the Nous eval. Muse Glimmer and Gemma ran at 0.6. Terminal-Bench figures come from different harnesses. Weights ship in BF16 on Hugging Face . No hosted inference provider serves the model yet. Community GGUF quants run in llama.cpp, LM Studio and Ollama, from 8.64 GB to 53.81 GB. The GGUF build also includes the image projector. Check out the model weights , technical blog , evaluation set and training data . item.title: Which Routing Does Each MoE Model Use? DeepSeek, Qwen, Mixtral, Llama 4, gpt-oss Compared
item.abstract: Open Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models share one idea but disagree on almost every routing detail. Expert counts range from 8 to 384. Top-k ranges from 1 to 8. Some models keep an always-on shared expert; others drop it. Every model below uses token-choice routing: each token selects its own experts. They differ on 5 knobs. These are expert count, experts per token, shared experts, the scoring function and the load-balancing method. The table lists each knob per model. Sources: each model’s Hugging Face config.json, model card or technical report, verified November 7, 2026. Configs and cards for Qwen3.6 and Llama 4 omit gating. gpt-oss and Llama 4 omit the balancing method. DeepSeek-V3 scores 256 routed experts with a sigmoid, then normalizes the selected scores. A per-expert bias steers the top-8 selection without touching the mixing weights. Experts sit in 8 groups, and the router keeps 4 groups first. Each token reaches at most 4 nodes, according to the technical report . One shared expert runs for every token. DeepSeek-V4 raises Pro to 384 routed experts but lowers top-k from 8 to 6. The score function becomes sqrtsoftplus. The first 3 MoE layers use hash routing , a fixed token-to-expert map. Bias-based noaux_tc balancing stays. Both original Qwen3 MoE models use 128 experts and route each token to 8. Qwen3 dropped the shared experts of Qwen2.5-MoE and adopted a global-batch balancing loss. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B changes course: 256 experts, 8 routed plus 1 shared, per its model card . Llama 4 Maverick alternates dense and MoE layers. In each MoE layer, a token goes to 1 shared expert and 1 of 128 routed experts. That top-1 design echoes the Switch Transformer. It keeps 17B active parameters despite 400B in total. gpt-oss-120b uses a linear router over 128 experts and keeps the top 4. Its config lists no shared expert. Its MoE weights ship in MXFP4, which lets the 117B model fit on a single 80 GB GPU. Kimi K2 ships with the DeepseekV3ForCausalLM architecture class and the noaux_tc router. It raises routed experts to 384 at the same top-8. The Kimi K2 report found that higher sparsity lowered loss at fixed active compute. GLM-4.5 chose 160 experts and more layers instead, favoring depth over width. More experts per layer means more weights resident in memory and more all-to-all traffic. Lower top-k, as in DeepSeek-V4, trims per-token compute and communication. Shared experts add a dense path that every token pays for. Check these fields before sizing GPUs for any MoE deployment. Model sources: DeepSeek-V4-Pro , DeepSeek-V3 report , Qwen3 report , Kimi K2 report , GLM-4.5 report , Mixtral paper . Also see gpt-oss-120b and the Llama 4 announcement . item.title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment
item.abstract:
All posts Count the memory formats on your machine List every place your coding tools keep something they "remember". A typical setup today: an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md in most repos, and .cursor/rules/*.mdc in a few an agent writing files to a /memories directory through Anthropic's memory tool Copilot keeping facts about each repo on GitHub's side a memory MCP server keeping a JSONL knowledge graph That's four different shapes, and none of them can read the others . A lesson your CI agent learns stays in whatever wrote it. Your editor agent can't read it, and neither can the next tool you try. Each format is reasonable on its own. Together, they rebuild the same small idea again and again: a note an agent left for its future self, stored at some address, true for a while. And the list keeps growing. Browse r/ClaudeAI, r/LocalLLaMA or r/cursor and you'll find a steady stream of "I built a memory layer for my agent" posts, each with its own storage, its own schema and its own MCP tools. That's good evidence the problem is real: people keep hitting it badly enough to build something. But every new solution adds one more format that nothing else can read. The problem isn't a missing tool. It's a missing agreement , and that only comes from the community working on it together. I build one of these tools, LoreKit, which is open source. This isn't a pitch that LoreKit has solved memory. Its format is one proposal among several, with gaps of its own. The point is that this is the moment to agree on a shared shape , and that another field has already shown how. We've seen this before Before 2019, every observability vendor shipped its own agent, its own instrumentation library and its own data format. Switching vendors meant instrumenting your code again. Two open projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, tried to fix that and competed with each other too. In 2019 they merged into OpenTelemetry . What mattered was what the vendors agreed to stop competing on: A data model : what a span, a metric and a log record are. Semantic conventions : shared names like service.name and http.* . A protocol : OTLP, one way to send the data. Reference implementations : shared SDKs and the Collector. Vendors kept competing on what they do with the data: storage, querying, analysis. Users instrument once. I work with OpenTelemetry every day at Dash0 , and that agreement is why a whole ecosystem of tools can read each other's data. The same four layers. Observability agreed on them and competes on what happens after the data arrives. Agent memory has plenty of implementations, but nothing agreed underneath them. Agent memory is where observability was before 2019. The timing is good: the formats are young enough to change, and there's already a neutral home for agent standards. MCP and AGENTS.md both sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation. A tour of the shapes These change quickly, so treat the details as a snapshot from late 2026. Family Example The unit of memory Addressed by Forgetting Instruction files AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , Cursor .mdc rules A whole Markdown file File path (plus globs for Cursor) Never. A person edits it Agent-managed files Anthropic's memory tool A file under /memories A path the model picks Never, unless the model deletes it Hosted repo facts GitHub Copilot Memory A fact with code citations One repository Deleted after 28 days unused Context blocks Letta core memory A labeled block with a character limit A label on an agent Never. Always in context Extracted facts Mem0 A fact the service extracts from messages user_id / agent_id / run_id / app_id Optional expiration date Namespaced store LangGraph BaseStore A JSON value dict A namespace tuple + key Optional TTL, reset when the item is read (by default) Knowledge graph MCP reference memory server Entities, relations, observations Entity name Never Temporal graph Graphiti / Zep A fact on a graph edge Entities + edge Facts are invalidated rather than deleted, on two timelines Addressed record LoreKit A record with a scope, key and lifecycle A scope string + key Never, unless a TTL is set A few of them got something right that a shared spec should keep. Copilot Memory pairs citations you can check against the code with forgetting by default, though it's locked inside one product. LangGraph shows how small the core can be: put(namespace, key, value) . Graphiti models time properly, with separate timelines for when a fact was true and when it was recorded. And AGENTS.md shows that a plain file at a known path can become a standard. The proposals that already exist Several people have started on this. MacPaw Research's Portable Memory is a .mem bundle with byte-reproducible serialization, deletion tombstones and optional signing; its authors say it isn't widely adopted yet. The Open Memory Protocol is an April 2026 draft for moving conversations and the memories derived from them between platforms as a ZIP with a manifest. Cognee's COGX format imports from Mem0, Letta and Zep. These mostly solve export : moving one person's memory from vendor A to vendor B. Coding tools also have a second, open problem: live addressing . When a CI job, an editor agent and a review bot work in the same repo at once, how do they read and write the same place and agree on what it means? A complete spec needs both. Export moves one owner's memory between vendors. Live addressing lets many tools share one place at the same time. The existing proposals focus on the first. A shared address could sit inside their records to cover the second. What a shared spec could look like Strip away the branding and every format answers the same four questions differently: where a memory is true, what its identity is (does a second write update it or duplicate it?), what it says , and when it stops being true . Nobody disagrees that those matter. The tools only disagree on the answers, which is where OpenTelemetry started too. There's one real fork: who writes the memory . In instruction files it's a person. In the memory tool, Letta and LoreKit, it's the model. In Mem0 and Graphiti, a service extracts facts from the conversation. A spec doesn't need to pick one. It needs to record which, so a reader knows how much to trust what it reads. Here's roughly what one record could look like as a file. It illustrates the data model; the field names aren't a proposal: --- spec : agent-memory/0.1 id : 8f0c2a6e-4b1d-4c7a-9e2f-3a5b6c7d8e9f address : { level : repo , value : github.com/acme/checkout } key : tests-need-local-postgres kind : lesson written_by : { type : agent , name : claude-code } content_type : text/markdown lifecycle : { expires_at : null , extended_by : write } attributes : { vcs.pr : 482 , ci.run_url : "https://ci.example/runs/123" } --- Integration tests fail with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432` unless Postgres is already running. Start it before `pnpm test` : docker compose up -d db The test setup does not start it for you. The frontmatter is the envelope: address and key say where it's true, id is its identity, lifecycle says when it stops, and written_by answers the fork. The Markdown below it is the memory itself, and content_type tells a reader how to treat it. Anything else a tool needs goes in attributes , under a namespace other tools can ignore. The same record serialises to JSON just as well, for a tool that wants to send it over the wire. Around that record, a spec would mirror OpenTelemetry's layers: Conventions : shared names for address levels ( global , project , repo , branch , and whatever monorepos need), for kinds, and for attribute namespaces ( vcs.* , ci.* , agent.* ), in one versioned registry. A contract : a few operations (write, read, list, search, archive) with fixed inputs and outputs, exposed over MCP. Many memory servers now offer an MCP interface, but each exposes different tools with different meanings.

(156 points, 101 comments on Hacker News)

item.title: MoE Routing Strategies Explained: Top-K, Expert-Choice, Sigmoid Gating and Dynamic Routing (2026 Guide)
item.abstract: Every Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model repeats one decision for every token: which experts should process it. That decision belongs to the router. MoE routing strategies shape quality, load balance and serving cost in every major open model. This guide explains the 7 routing strategies used in production, and the models that use each one. MoE routing is the mechanism that sends each token to a small subset of expert networks. A router scores every expert, keeps the top candidates and weights their outputs. Only the selected experts run. Mixtral 8x7B , for example, gives each token access to 47B parameters but uses 13B active parameters. Each token scores all experts with a linear layer and keeps the k highest. A softmax over those k scores sets the mixing weights. Mixtral picks 2 of 8 experts. gpt-oss-120b picks 4 of 128. Qwen3-235B-A22B picks 8 of 128. An auxiliary loss usually keeps expert load even. Used by: Mixtral, gpt-oss, Qwen3. Switch Transformer showed that routing each token to 1 expert preserves quality and cuts router compute. Each expert gets a fixed buffer: tokens per batch divided by experts, times a capacity factor. Overflow tokens skip the layer through the residual connection. Llama 4 Maverick also sends each token to 1 routed expert, plus a shared expert. Used by: Switch Transformer, Llama 4 Maverick (with a shared expert). DeepSeekMoE splits each layer into always-on shared experts and sparsely routed experts. The shared expert captures common knowledge, so routed experts can specialize. DeepSeek-V3 uses 1 shared and 256 routed experts, activating 8. Kimi K2 , GLM-4.5 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B follow the same pattern. Qwen3 went the other way and removed shared experts . Used by: DeepSeek-V3 and V4, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5, Qwen3.6, Llama 4. DeepSeek-V3 scores experts with a sigmoid instead of a softmax. It adds a per-expert bias only when choosing the top-k. After each step, the bias drops for overloaded experts and rises for idle ones. Mixing weights still come from the raw scores. GLM-4.5 uses loss-free balance routing with sigmoid gates . DeepSeek-V4 switches the score to sqrtsoftplus but keeps bias balancing. Used by: DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-4.5, Kimi K2. Sending one token to experts on many nodes is expensive. DeepSeek-V3 caps each token at 4 nodes, chosen by their highest affinity scores. Its config splits experts into 8 groups and keeps 4 before the final top-8 pick. DeepSeek says this cap lets training nearly fully overlap computation and communication. Kimi K2 drops grouping entirely, with n_group set to 1. Google’s expert choice routing flips the direction. Each expert picks its top-k tokens, so every expert gets a fixed bucket size. Tokens can receive a variable number of experts. The paper reports more than 2x faster training convergence. The catch is causality: a token’s expert can depend on later tokens. DeepSeek researchers measured an abnormal loss drop of about 10% from this leakage. Used by: Research and non-causal settings. None of the 10 models in our companion table uses it. Hash routing assigns experts from the token ID, with no learned router. DeepSeek-V4 uses hash routing in its first 3 MoE layers . Dynamic top-k lets the number of active experts vary per token. SMIDT built it into SGLang and improved P99 time-to-first-token by 1.21 to 1.26x. Used by: DeepSeek-V4 (hash routing), research serving systems (dynamic top-k). Most teams do not pick a router. They inherit one when they choose a checkpoint. Before serving, read 4 fields in config.json: expert count, experts per token, shared experts and topk_method. Changing top-k at inference changes the model itself, so treat it as a quality experiment. For new pretraining runs, sigmoid scoring with bias balancing is the current open default. Check out the primary sources: Switch Transformer , Expert Choice , Loss-Free Balancing , DeepSeek-V3 report and the DeepSeek-V4 model card . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? item.title: Goodbye Claude, hello Pi
item.abstract:
I’ve been a longtime Claude Code user, ever since it became available in the Claude Pro subscription plan over a year ago. I remember the first time I used it, feeling giddy as it spat out messy Python code for whatever random weekend project I was working on, all from a single prompt. I’m certain that in a few years we’ll all look back at its release as one of the major drivers of this new era of software development we’re in. Despite this, due to an accumulation of many small frustrations, I’ve finally decided to retire it as my main coding harness and migrate my development setup to use Pi instead. Someone at Anthropic must’ve caught wind… just a day after making my decision, they announced Claude Code would finally start supporting AGENTS.md files in an effort to get me to stay. Unfortunately, for me it was too little, too late. In lieu of a proper obituary, I’d like to take this time to say a few words about the things I liked least about Claude Code (and thus what I’m looking forward to avoiding with Pi). The AGENTS.md thing kind of epitomizes the whole reason I decided to quit using Claude Code. Don’t get me wrong, having a ton of CLAUDE.md files scattered about various GitHub hobby repos is great guerrilla marketing. But it sucks for users to have to deal with copying or symlinking between the two formats. Like the Luddite I am, I still prefer to review most of the code it churns out before I commit it. I use(d) Claude Code inside VSCode, and it lets you connect the harness to the IDE. This is nice because you can highlight text in a file and have it automatically included in the context when asking questions or requesting changes during a review. Except you can only have one session “connected” to the IDE at a time. If you open a second tab to start another task while the first one works, it can’t receive the text selection events from the IDE at all. This has been reported at least as far back as December 2025 … and closed as a duplicate of a totally unrelated bug. 1 Of course, you can always use the official Claude Code VSCode GUI extension, which does allow you to have multiple tabs open and load the text selection into the context of each. But this extension has plenty of problems of its own. Half of the built-in slash commands don’t work at all in the GUI. It doesn’t have any support for a custom status line. Subagent output messages are simply layered into the main chat thread in chronological order, which is a mess to read when more than one is running. I could go on and on. In spite of all of these existing issues, it seems like Anthropic has worked at a feverish pace to pack more features into Claude Code without much care for quality or stability. Dynamic workflows , agent teams , ultrareviews – all great ways to help enterprise customers burn ever more tokens each day, but not really anything I want or need. Alongside all of these feature releases, they always seem to be fiddling with things in ways that mess up my personal setup. At the time of writing, there have been 244 releases to Claude Code this year; over 3/4 of these changed the system prompt or tool descriptions, which can substantially change how the LLM performs (especially when these new instructions contradict user prompts or repo conventions). And what are all those changes for? Despite chopping 80% of the system prompt , Claude Code still has way more overhead than Pi for seemingly no benefit. The default Bash tool’s description is almost 3,000 tokens, most of which is random stuff about using git and opening PRs on GitHub. 2 The models already know how to do this without detailed instructions, by the way. 3 This post has been a lot of hating. I’m sorry! That’s not my usual style, and I do think Anthropic has made a really cool piece of software here. I’m also not under any delusion that I would’ve done a better job if I were the one in charge of running Claude Code from the beginning. LLM coding harnesses are a very new space and being one of the first to innovate in a field is a really hard task. Later tools like Pi have the benefit of hindsight to see what works and what doesn’t, what’s a core feature and what can be cut. Ultimately, CC feels like a product without a strong vision or direction. It’s as if a bunch of excited engineers and PMs are rapidly tacking on whatever features suit their workflow… but without consideration for how this might make things worse for other users. It seems like there isn’t someone high-up whose job is strictly to say “no” to these requests, which is incredibly important when it comes to product engineering. So, for now, I’m leaving. I’m excited to lean more into Pi. The first few days required some finagling, but since then it’s been smooth sailing. I’m enjoying the stability, minimalist approach, and the extreme level of customizability. I’ve already written a couple of extensions to support my use cases, which I’m hoping to share soon after I’ve cleaned them up a bit. If you’re also feeling these frustrations, I’d highly encourage giving an open source harness a try! It’s not like there’s some huge technical roadblock to this either. After installing Pi, I wrote an extension to handle this very functionality across multiple open tabs in like 20 minutes. (return) Bonus points for the fact that it instructs the model to use cat <<'EOF' which (prior to widespread rollout of auto mode) would always trip the manual review rules regardless of existing git command allowlists. (return) If you assume 1 million DAU and 100M requests per day, trimming 1,000 tokens off of this could literally save millions of dollars in inference costs per year. Surely that’s worth some engineer’s time?? (return) I love hearing people's thoughts, so please don't hesitate to shoot me an email at calebdotsoftware@gmail.com . If you'd like to get updates whenever I publish a new post, you can subscribe over email or with RSS . If you want to comment or read the public discussion about this post, I've shared it on the following sites: Twitter , Mastodon , Bluesky Created 21 Sep 2026 · Updated 07 Nov 2026 · Build 2f1e49

(628 points, 405 comments on Hacker News)

item.title: 🗞️Apple AI Taps Qwen, Tencent’s Hy4, and China’s AI Chip Squeeze
item.abstract: China AI Weekly Digest summarizes the week’s big news, model updates, compute, policy, products, and research, drawn from the China AI Index newsfeed . The digest is (mostly) compiled and drafted by an AI agent using credible news outlets; I fact-check and edit it. Read to the end for “One to Watch” as this week’s video pick. This week: 181 stories tracked (2 editor picks, 59 English-language, 120 Chinese-language 🇨🇳) over 2026-10-30–2026-11-06. Apple begins testing Qwen inside Apple Intelligence in China. Apple opened developer testing this week ahead of a planned December rollout with iOS 27.3. Alibaba’s Qwen will be available through Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, giving users a way to ask about a photo or document without starting in a separate chatbot. The integration is opt-in, and users can choose what to send to Qwen. For Alibaba, the distribution matters as much as the model: Qwen gets a place in everyday iPhone workflows, even when users never open its app. ( SCMP / 雷峰網 ) Tencent brings vision and computer use to Hy4, with WorkBuddy as its proving ground. The November 4 release adds visual reasoning and computer use to Tencent’s flagship model. In a hands-on test, Chinese media ifanr gave WorkBuddy a gameplay recording and used Hy4 to build a playable browser prototype. Users can show the agent what they want it to build. Tencent still acknowledges a gap with leading proprietary systems on some difficult research and coding tasks. Hosted access started with the launch; Tencent said the final weights and system cards would follow. ( SCMP / 愛範兒 / @TencentHunyuan ) Chinese AI buyers run into separate bottlenecks for overseas GPU rentals and chip deliveries. The FT reports that Oracle dropped an estimated $7 billion, five-year deal to give Tencent access to as many as 100,000 AI chips in Southeast Asia after US officials raised concerns. Separately, CNBC reports that Moonshot explored renting Nvidia Blackwell capacity in Europe; those talks don’t establish a signed lease. Bloomberg reports that Chinese buyers expect about 1% of roughly $70 billion in RTX orders over the next four months. ( FT / CNBC / Bloomberg ) Baidu and Moonshot published weights, while Ant and Meituan introduced models built for longer tasks involving images and tools. Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, a mixture-of-experts model with 280 billion total parameters and 14 billion active per token. Baidu says it supports up to a million tokens during fine-tuning and inference. This is a base checkpoint developers can adapt for their own tasks. ( 量子位 ) Moonshot published the Kimi K3.1 Pro weights on Hugging Face this week, following the October launch through its own products and API. The download gives developers a self-hosting option for the 2.8 trillion-parameter model. ( @Kimi_Moonshot ) Ant announced Ling-3.2-flash, a multimodal model with 560 billion total parameters and 25 billion active. Its stated targets include complex visual tasks, 3D interaction and medical reasoning. ( @AntLingAGI ) Meituan launched LongCat-2.5, a natively multimodal model with 1.6 trillion total parameters and about 48 billion active. The company is targeting tasks that take many steps, including coding projects where the agent needs to inspect visual output as it works. ( 雷峰網 / @Meituan_LongCat ) Domestic compute news spanned model training, server memory, optical links and chips for running models on devices. DeepSeek plans to pretrain its next model on Huawei Ascend chips, Chinese media reports, citing supply-chain sources. Pretraining would put Ascend to work earlier in the model-development process than inference deployments do. ( 財聯社 ) CXMT plans to send customers samples of server DRAM built on its 4F² architecture by year-end. This is a separate development from its HBM3E effort. CXMT hasn’t set a mass-production date and says commercialization depends on customer validation and demand. ( SCMP ) Hua Hong plans to expand silicon-photonics capacity as part of its next major expansion in 2027. Chairman Bai Peng singled out components for optical modules and power-management chips, two areas where the foundry wants to add capacity. ( SCMP ) Houmo Intelligence reportedly closed a Series B worth several billion yuan. The chipmaker plans to expand deliveries of its M50 edge inference processor and develop its next compute-in-memory products. Houmo says the M50 has been selected for more than 150 customer designs, a measure of adoption that precedes shipments. ( 雷峰網 ) Moffett AI closed a Series C+ of nearly RMB1 billion, according to Qbit. The chipmaker specializes in sparse inference and has adapted two remote-sensing models to its accelerator cards with a Peking University research partner—a specific application for hardware designed to skip unnecessary calculations. ( 量子位 ) The robotics rounds backed specific industrial jobs: moving goods around sites and loading and unloading them. Yicheng Innovation completed a RMB200 million Series C for its industrial autonomous-vehicle business. Its vehicles move materials around sites such as factories, logistics parks and ports. The company plans to use the proceeds to expand manufacturing capacity, improve the technology and deploy more vehicles. ( 投資界 ) Qingtian Intelligence closed a Pre-A round worth tens of millions of yuan for robots that load and unload goods. Its industrial investors are also helping it test in operating logistics sites, giving the company a route from pilot installations to deployments across multiple facilities. ( 投資界 ) Beijing signaled work on a broad AI law, while more targeted measures addressed employment and eldercare. China’s National Development and Reform Commission said it would accelerate work on comprehensive AI legislation and develop safety standards and ethical rules covering the technology’s lifecycle. The November 3 briefing signals a legislative priority; China has yet to enact a unified national AI law. ( 財新 ) Six departments issued measures encouraging the use of embodied AI, language models, brain–computer interfaces and exoskeletons in eldercare. The measures focus on developing uses for age-friendly products and services; they do not establish clinical effectiveness or authorize any particular device. ( 財聯社 ) Hello China Tech puts the State Council’s recent AI employment guidance alongside a Hangzhou dismissal case. The guidance encourages advance notice and help moving workers into new roles. As the analysis points out, protecting workers with existing contracts leaves a separate question: how many entry-level jobs companies will offer in the first place. ( Hello China Tech ) Agents showed up in phone demos, research desks and even a Singles’ Day livestream. DeepSeek showcased Creator Mode in Harness, where users can describe a plugin and have the agent build it for use inside the app. The company shared prompts for seven demos, including a design workspace and a sandbox game. Creator Mode is distinct from the Super-agent research prototype below. ( Bloomberg / 投資界 ) Doubao Work removed its five-hour usage cap for personal subscribers on November 6. Weekly allowances still apply. The change lets someone spend more of their existing allowance on a long task in one sitting without waiting for the shorter window to reset. ( 雷峰網 ) StepFun’s device arm showed the STEPX Neo agent phone at Qualcomm’s booth at the China International Import Expo. Demos included checking Alipay offers, making travel videos with Jianying and planning trips through Ctrip. The expo appearance was a demonstration; retail availability wasn’t established. ( 量子位 ) Alibaba Cloud introduced Qovest, a workbench for investment research. It retrieves data, gathers sources, generates reports and can revisit a subject on a schedule, keeping the results in a shared research workspace. Individual access began through invitation testing; an enterprise edition is planned.

item.title: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
item.abstract: AI News Tech Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks. Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 8, 2026, 7:18 PM UTC Photo: David Imel / The Verge Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals. Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example. But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says: Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.
